label: School worksheet
source: Loyola International School Grade 6 practice worksheet (Ch 4)

questions.q: Which step comes first in organising data?
questions.e: First collect, then organise (classify/tally), then present (graph), then interpret.

questions.q: What does the height (or length) of a bar in a bar graph show?
questions.a: The frequency or value it stands for
w: The total of all the data
questions.e: Bars are all the same width; only their height shows the value.

questions.q: A pictograph represents data using…
questions.e: Each picture stands for a fixed number – read the key.

questions.q: What is data?
questions.a: A collection of numbers or facts gathered to give some information
questions.e: Data can be organised in tables and shown as pictographs or bar graphs.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Primary data are more reliable than secondary data.
Reason (R): Primary data are collected directly by the investigator for a specific purpose.
questions.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
w: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
questions.e: Because you collect it yourself for your purpose, you know exactly how it was gathered.

questions.q: Data collected by an investigator for the first time is called…
questions.e: Data taken from books, websites or reports collected by others is secondary data.

questions.q: An observation that occurs 7 times is recorded with tally marks as…
questions.a: one bundle of five (four lines crossed by a fifth) and two more lines
w: seven separate lines in a row
one bundle of five and seven lines
questions.e: Tally marks are grouped in fives: 5 + 2 = 7.

questions.q: In a pictograph, each symbol must represent…
questions.e: The key tells you the fixed value of every symbol.

questions.q: You want to show the heights of the tallest person in each class. Which bar graph fits best?
questions.a: Vertical bars – heights are naturally measured upwards
w: Horizontal bars – heights must be sideways
It is not possible to draw
questions.e: Vertical bars match how we see height in real life.

questions.q: You are showing the longest river on each continent and its length. Which bar graph fits best?
questions.a: Horizontal bars – long names fit and lengths read left to right
questions.e: Horizontal bars suit long labels and ‘length’ data.

questions.q: By how many did the number of tigers increase from 2006 to 2022?
questions.passage: Number of tigers in India (approx.): 2006 – 1400, 2010 – 1700, 2014 – 2200, 2018 – 3000, 2022 – 3700. (Project Tiger was launched in 1973; exact counts began in 2006.)

questions.q: Between which two survey years did the number of tigers increase the most?
questions.e: Increases: +300, +500, +800, +700. The biggest jump is 2014 → 2018.
questions.passage: Number of tigers in India (approx.): 2006 – 1400, 2010 – 1700, 2014 – 2200, 2018 – 3000, 2022 – 3700. (Project Tiger was launched in 1973; exact counts began in 2006.)

questions.q: Shagufta and Divya drew the bar for 2014 at about 2900 and the bar for 2018 at about 2200. What is the mistake?
questions.a: The two bars are the wrong heights – 2014 should be 2200 and 2018 should be 3000
w: The years should be in reverse order
questions.e: Always check each bar against the table before finishing.
questions.passage: Number of tigers in India (approx.): 2006 – 1400, 2010 – 1700, 2014 – 2200, 2018 – 3000, 2022 – 3700. (Project Tiger was launched in 1973; exact counts began in 2006.)

questions.q: The graph paper has 10 squares up the side. Which scale is best for the tiger data?
questions.e: 3700 needs a top value above 3700: 10 × 500 = 5000 fits; 10 × 100 = 1000 is too small; 5000 per square makes tiny bars.
questions.passage: Number of tigers in India (approx.): 2006 – 1400, 2010 – 1700, 2014 – 2200, 2018 – 3000, 2022 – 3700. (Project Tiger was launched in 1973; exact counts began in 2006.)

questions.q: Car wash pictograph (one car symbol = {k} cars). How many cars were washed on Saturday?
questions.e: Saturday has {s} symbols × {k} = {ans} cars.

questions.q: Car wash pictograph (one car symbol = {k} cars). How many more cars were washed on Saturday than on Friday?
questions.e: ({s} − {f}) symbols × {k} = {ans} cars.

questions.q: Car wash pictograph (one car symbol = {k} cars). How many cars were washed over all three days?
questions.e: ({f} + {s} + {u}) symbols × {k} = {ans} cars.

questions.q: How many times did Rakesh get 5?
questions.e: Tally the 5s: 11.

questions.q: Which outcome occurred the fewest times?
Which outcome occurred the most times?
questions.e: 5 appears 11 times.

questions.q: How many times did he get an even number (2, 4 or 6)?
How many times did he get 1?
questions.e: Tally the 1s: 7.

questions.q: What is the difference between the most frequent and the least frequent outcome counts?
questions.e: Most: 5 (11 times). Least: 4 (4 times). 11 − 4 = 7.

questions.q: In a class, {m} students like Maths, {s} like Science, {e} like English, {ss} like Social Studies and {ar} like Art. How many students like Maths or English?
In a class, {m} students like Maths, {s} like Science, {e} like English, {ss} like Social Studies and {ar} like Art. How many students are in the class?
questions.e: Add all the groups: {m} + {s} + {e} + {ss} + {ar} = {ans}.

questions.q: In a class, {m} students like Maths and {ar} like Art. {x} new students join and all of them like Art. How many more students like Maths than Art now?
questions.e: Art now has {ar} + {x} students; Maths has {m}. Difference = {m} − {ar} − {x} = {ans}.
